articles.title: Trump again pushes Saudi Arabia to Accept Israel’s Help against Houthis - Daily Pakistan
articles.summary: Trump again pushes Saudi Arabia to Accept Israel’s Help against Houthis  Daily Pakistan
articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD – US President Donald Trump made a striking pitch to Saudi Arabia to accept Israel’s help against Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
Calling Israeli support very helpful, Trump hinted that a Saudi-Israeli normalization deal could be closer than ever, even as Riyadh maintains that Palestinian statehood remains key and Iran offers to help end the conflict.
US President Donald Trump urged Saudi Arabia to accept Israel’s assistance against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, adding a new dimension to regional tensions as speculation grows over a possible normalization agreement between Riyadh and Tel Aviv.
Trump was asked whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli support in operations against the Houthis. “Yes, absolutely. Israel has been very helpful to Saudi Arabia,” he replied, hinting at cooperation between two countries amid continuing regional security concerns.
Trump’s remarks also revived questions about whether Saudi Arabia could move closer to formally normalizing relations with Israel, a diplomatic breakthrough that has remained elusive despite previous efforts backed by Washington.
Asked whether Saudi Arabia’s potential entry into the Abraham Accords was being reconsidered, Trump expressed optimism, saying, “Yes, I think it could happen. Perhaps it is even more likely than before.” He called Abraham Accords “one of our great achievements,” referring to the agreements brokered through US efforts in 2020 that established or normalized relations between Israel and several Arab countries.
Trump further claimed that Saudi Arabia was pleased with the support of both Israel and the United States.
Before Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, Saudi Arabia and Israel had been widely viewed as moving closer to a possible normalization agreement. However, the diplomatic landscape has since been complicated by the Gaza war and the wider regional conflict.
Riyadh has consistently maintained that clear progress toward the establishment of a Palestinian state is necessary for normalizing relations with Israel, making the future of any agreement dependent on broader political and security considerations.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also made comments that have drawn attention to the possibility of regional cooperation. Asked in an interview with Israeli media on Tuesday whether Saudi Arabia had requested assistance from Israel, Netanyahu responded, according to The Times of Israel, “There is hardly a state in the Middle East that is not asking us for help.”
His remarks came amid heightened attention to the security implications of Houthi activities and the potential role of Israel in addressing threats facing countries across the region.
However, Netanyahu’s statement, as reported, did not explicitly confirm that Saudi Arabia had formally requested Israeli assistance.
Meanwhile, Iran rejected allegations linking it to Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and expressed readiness to help resolve the conflict if the relevant parties request its involvement.

articles.title: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia  Al JazeeraEgypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked  ReutersEgypt's Sissi says he'll defend Saudi Arabia, if asked  DW.comEgypt said to mull supporting defense of Saudi Arabia in face of Houthi attacks  The Times of IsraelEgypt prepared to defend Saudi Arabia after deadly Houthi airport attack  New York Post
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.
Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.
“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.
“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”
Attacks on Saudi Arabia
The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.
El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.
A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
Red Sea security
That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.
Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.
They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.
Sisi’s future
Speaking to recruits at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital on Saturday, el-Sisi also confirmed that he would not seek to extend his presidency beyond 2030, in line with the Egyptian constitution.
“The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive,” he said.
He added that his decision is “completely settled” and there will be “no discussion” about it.
Egypt’s constitution was updated in 2019 to increase term length to six years from four, and to allow el-Sisi to run for another six-year term in 2023. That means his term is due to expire in 2030, and he is not allowed to run again.
He said the Egyptian constitution “would not be touched”.

articles.title: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means  Al JazeeraIran-aligned Houthis launch deadly attack on Yemeni presidential palace in escalating campaign against Saudi Arabia  CNNMissiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu  ReutersIran war updates: Five killed, 16 hurt in Houthi attack on palace in Aden  Al JazeeraHouthi Missiles Strike Government Headquarters in Yemen  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday.
On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo.
Recommended Stories
After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.
The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war, largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?
Here’s what you need to know:
What happened at Maashiq Palace?
The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.
Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.
The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.
What happened at the airport?
On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.
Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.
The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.
Why are attacks on Aden significant?
Aden is the interim capital of Yemen.
The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.
The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.
The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.
But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.
Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
The city has been hit before.
In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.
A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.
What reaction has there been?
On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.
He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.
Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.
Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.
“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.
The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.
What is happening in the wider conflict?
Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.
Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.
The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.
On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.
In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.
Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Defy Difference in Military Power
By Gerry Doyle (Bloomberg) — The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are demonstrating the limits of the kingdom’s military prowess — despite defense spending that far outstrips that of its regional neighbors.
Missiles and drones fired by the Iran-backed group from Yemen have wreaked havoc in Saudi Arabia in recent days, killing at least 18 people and forcing the closure of the country’s main international airport in Riyadh. The Houthis are showing no sign of scaling back their campaign, targeting several Saudi Arabian cities in an assault this week that’s continued into Thursday.
Saudi Arabia allocated between $64 billion and $96 billion this year for defense, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Economics. The upper end is more than twice as much as Israel, the next biggest Middle East spender.
Video Muted
The kingdom operates Raytheon Co. Patriot missile batteries with the latest Lockheed Martin Corp. PAC-3 interceptors, flies hundreds of Boeing Co. F-15 fighters customized for its air force, and is the only Gulf country with mid-air refueling aircraft.
One reason the Houthis have been able to cause such destruction with less advanced equipment is Saudi Arabia’s size, which complicates defense efforts.The kingdom covers more than 2.1 million square kilometers (830,000 square miles), with many strategic targets to protect, from oil infrastructure to air bases to several large cities.
Defending against ballistic missiles is complex when protecting a single target, let alone sites sprinkled across a vast country. Thousands of Iranian strikes across the Arabian peninsula during the initial phase of the US and Israeli war on the Islamic Republic were largely thwarted by missile defenses, but even a 90% success rate can mean massive damage on the ground.
Saudi Arabia’s military is also still in the process of modernizing and remains heavily reliant on the US for military intelligence.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.
The most recent rounds of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have tended to involve a mix of weapons that further complicate defensive efforts: small drones, low-flying, cheap cruise missiles and ballistic missiles.
In addition, the Houthis are a nimble, rapidly evolving opponent backed by Iran, capable of building and deploying missiles and drones that can challenge even advanced defense systems. Years of fighting in Yemen mean the group is battle hardened, resisting protracted military efforts to dislodge or contain them.
“The Houthis are partly beneficiaries of good fortune, but they seem remarkably adaptive,” said Ankit Panda, Stanton Senior Fellow in the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “A determined attacker armed with missiles is still difficult to deal with.”
The Houthi arsenal has now evolved to the point where the group can manufacture relatively precise drones and ballistic missiles — some of which rely on parts from Chinese companies. Those munitions might cost thousands, or hundreds of thousands of dollars, far cheaper than the multimillion-dollar air defense interceptors used to stop them.
That means even a successfully intercepted attack imposes further costs on Saudi Arabia, and makes it more vulnerable to future strikes.
Defensive weapons such as the Iranian-made 358 surface-to-air missiles — which can loiter at high altitudes and strike subsonic aircraft — make the skies over Yemen dangerous too.
Another issue, said Bloomberg Economics defense lead Becca Wasser, is that Patriot air defense batteries are directional. They do not cover a 360-degree area, so if radars and launchers were positioned to intercept Iranian fire, they may not have been able to easily shoot down Houthi missiles, she said.
Air and missile capabilities have improved as part of Saudi Arabia’s modernization efforts, Wasser said. Although pilots learned considerably from the long Yemen air war, their aircraft remain largely reliant on the US for targeting data, in particular.
The situation has improved since Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman began a reform agenda, alongside “real-life experience in its first war against Yemen,” Wasser said. “But modernization is slow and confined to pockets of bright spots rather than upskilling across the force.”
Although Riyadh has a fleet of more than 200 F-15 jets — almost as many as the US Air Force — it was unable to use them decisively in more than a decade of bombing the Houthis. Saudi Arabia went to war with the militant group in 2015 after it took control of the Yemeni capital, Saana, though fighting receded between a 2022 truce and the recent flare up.
“Equipment and funding do not win wars,” said Wolf-Christian Paes, a senior fellow for armed conflict at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. “Training, motivation and leadership do.”
US influence in the Middle East after 1990 — when Washington intervened after Iraq invaded Kuwait — prompted many countries in the region to rely on US firepower rather than fully develop their own capabilities.
Saudi Arabia was not immune to this “protection curse,” said David Roberts, a reader in international security and Middle East studies at King’s College London.
US struggles in Afghanistan, and incidents like the 2019 Houthi drone attack against oil facilities in Abqaiq, in the east of Saudi Arabia, punctured the image that “Uncle Sam would basically detect and protect,” Roberts said.
US President Donald Trump has so far opted against intervening directly in the current conflict. In a post on Truth Social on Tuesday he said the Houthis were “behaving very badly,” without specifying what action the US could take.
Saudi Oil Minister Prince Abdul Aziz Bin Salman said this week that “the events of recent weeks are serious,” adding that the kingdom’s response “must be equally serious, while remaining focused on the decades ahead.”
The Houthis began threatening shipping in the Red Sea after the start of the war in Gaza, which prompted the US to briefly intervene, launching more than 1,000 strikes over three months. But hunting down hidden, mobile launchers and shutting down buried production facilities is difficult, especially in the rugged terrain in which the Houthis operate. The operation ended with a ceasefire.
The Houthis show “there are very clear limits what an air campaign can do,” said April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Former US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, speaking at the Warsaw Defense Forum on Monday, said Saudi Arabia would most likely need help from friendly nations to counter the Houthi threat.
“There will be a concerted effort to get the Houthi thing under control,” he said. “But it won’t be easy. They are much more resilient than most people recognize.”
The conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have shown how the power of ballistic missiles, particularly those with a range of 1,000 kilometers or more, mean even countries whose millitaries are relatively weak can cause problems for more powerful adversaries.
The Houthis’ strike arsenal includes indigenously produced Quds-1 cruise missiles, which have a reach of about 750 kilometers, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Its homegrown ballistic arsenal is larger, with Burkan-1, -2, and -3 designs, which can fly 600 kilometers, 850 kilometers and 1,200 kilometers, respectively, giving the militants the range to hit nearly any site in Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh’s struggles to extinguish the Houthi threat and defend against counterattacks reflects the difficulty of a task many others have failed at too.
“Yemen is a hard nut to crack. The US couldn’t do it,” Longley Alley said. “This is something that can’t be solved with a military tool only.”
Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.
This weekend’s deadly attacks on Riyadh’s main airport have demonstrated the ability of Yemen’s Houthis to strike at the heart of Saudi power, raising the risk of a dangerous escalation that could draw in the US.

articles.title: How are Yemen's Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively? - The Economic Times
articles.summary: How are Yemen's Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe international investment hub as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil.
This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say.
They attribute Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, bolstering the ragtag Yemeni group, and the impact of the US war on Iran, which has depleted stocks of interceptors.
TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN
Iran has been giving weapons, money and training to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN arms embargo.
"Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted."
Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran.
"The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles.
"Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told a press conference the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.
DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY
A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don't rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran.
The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment.
"China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said.
The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons' effectiveness.
Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle.
WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS
While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular.
"Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute.
Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said.
WAR EXPERIENCE
The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said.
A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel's assault on Gaza in 2023, which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea.
The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities.
"They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated."

articles.title: Mohammed bin Salman faces most consequential test yet as Saudi Arabia comes under Houthi fire - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Mohammed bin Salman faces most consequential test yet as Saudi Arabia comes under Houthi fire  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Synopsis
Mohammed bin Salman is currently grappling with increasing Houthi attacks that threaten Saudi infrastructure and international stability. The Crown Prince's appeals for support from the United States have not succeeded in securing intervention. Increased tensions have led to major airlines suspending flights to Saudi Arabia, impacting travel plans. Efforts to forge alliances with Pakistan and Turkey have yielded limited results in countering the Houthi threat.
Also Read: Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point: Here's how
Multiple flights in Saudi Arabia remain grounded while Indian airlines Air India, IndiGo and Akasa Air have either extended or announced flight suspensions amid escalating regional tensions and disruptions to air travel.
Efforts to get backing from Trump have so far failed to secure direct American intervention, while a new defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey has only been able to provide limited help. Other states in the Gulf have verbally supported Saudi Arabia but not directly joined the armed resistance against the Houthis.
MBS had made a previous attempt to crush the Houthis
Mohammed bin Salman, or MBS, as he is called, had raged war against the group in 2015 but failed to defeat them. The Houthis have grown much stronger over the past decade while MBS, along with a Saudi-backed Yemeni coalition keep attacking.
By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions, the Houthis are seeking to pressure MBS to meet their demands in Yemen and push Trump to ease the blockade strangling Iran’s economy, as reported by Reuters.
The Houthis have previously launched massive strikes inside Saudi, especially a 2019 attack on oil giant Saudi Aramco's facilities that had, for the time being, stopped about 5% of oil supply.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, triggering a war that ended before a ceasefire was reached in 2022.
Where does Trump stand in all of this?
MBS, who has diplomatically and strategically backed Trump's administration is not getting the same thing in return. The crown prince increased Saudi Arabia's promised investments in the United States to $1 trillion last November and also signed a defence agreement. Bloomberg reported that the US administration was being reluctant to involve itself in this crisis and has asked Riyadh not to spark a major new conflict in Yemen as the war in Iran prevails.
The fighting with the Houthis has opened another front in the bigger conflict in Iran, adding to political pressures that the US is facing ahead of the midterm elections. The war has kept global energy prices elevated and driven up fuel costs in the United States, resulting in one of the primary election issues.
According to agencies, military attacks by Riyadh will hardly be able to get rid of the Houthi movement's threat. The militias have survived years of US and Israeli airstrikes. The Houthis intensified their attacks on shipping in Red Sea after Israel attacked Gaza and thereby affected global oil markets.
Also Read: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
The Houthis have not targeted American assets, and probably because direct attacks might risk violation of a ceasefire deal with the United States last year, after Washington struck more than 1,000 sites in Yemen.
The US blockade of Iranian ports, a part of American strategy in the wider Iran war, is also affecting a major chunk of Washington's resources in the region.
Speaking to reporters in Maryland on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack … and they have a right to defend themselves.”
A broader US-Iran war angle
Iran has provided the Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, with funding, arms, ammunition and training for over the last 10 years, though Iran has denied arming the group in breach of a UN arms embargo.
Despite Iran’s own financial and military pressures from the current situation, the now have Houthis the ability to make their own weapons, with Iranian assistance, according expert interviews by Reuters.
Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of fuelling a sharp escalation in the Houthis’ conflict with the kingdom, saying Tehran continued to arm and train the Yemeni group.
Speaking at a virtual briefing with reporters, Saudi Arabia’s deputy foreign minister for public diplomacy said Riyadh remained in contact with Tehran, but Iran appeared unwilling to make concessions.
What other geopolitical conflicts has MBS been part of
Mohammed bin Salman’s reign as Saudi'ss de facto ruler has been marked by a series of regional crises, from the earlier Yemen war and the confrontation with Iran to the attacks in 2019 on Saudi oil facilities and a diplomatic rift with Qatar.
The vulnerability of Riyadh's infrastructure was exposed in 2019, when attacks on the Abqaiq oil processing facility and Khurais oil field knocked out roughly half of the kingdom’s oil production. The Houthis claimed responsibility, while the United States and other assessments pointed to Iran.
MBS also faced a regional diplomatic setback in 2017, when Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt imposed a boycott on Qatar over allegations that it supported extremist groups and maintained close ties with Iran.
Further, Saudi has accused Iran of supporting armed groups, including the Houthis, while the two countries restored diplomatic relations in a China-brokered agreement in March 2023 after a seven-year break.

articles.title: Defending a Partner: Air Defense as Diplomacy in Israel–UAE Relations - E-International Relations
articles.summary: Defending a Partner: Air Defense as Diplomacy in Israel–UAE Relations  E-International Relations
articles.full_text:
In late April 2026, Axios reported that Israel had deployed an Iron Dome air defense battery to the United Arab Emirates along with Israel Defense Forces (IDF) personnel to operate it during the US-Israel-Iran War, particularly to help the country intercept Iranian missiles. The US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, later confirmed the deployment and attributed it to “an extraordinary relationship between the UAE and Israel based on the Abraham Accords.” The UAE acknowledged the gesture, with an Emirati official saying, “We are not going to forget it.”

This is the central question raised by the article, which will examine the deployment as an instrument of soft power. However, the problem that arises here is that soft power generally does not include military capabilities as a source of attraction since it is considered a part of a country’s hard power, i.e., achieving a country’s goals though coercion or inducement instead of attraction. However, the Emirati response suggests that the military deployment produced something closer to gratitude and goodwill – characteristics of soft power. This is the primary puzzle of this article – whether defensive military technologies can generate attraction and satisfy diplomatic goals, and if yes, under what circumstances, and what are the limits of such exchanges?
Two arguments are put forward by the article regarding this aspect.
Firstly, it argues that, unlike traditional soft power studies dictate, military technologies, primarily defensive, can be utilized as diplomatic instruments when it follows the three conditions of transfer, co-development, and deployment.
Such an argument is based on the concepts of defense diplomacy and arms transfers as diplomacy that considers military cooperation and assistance as instruments of foreign policy.
It further draws upon Nye’s soft power theory, especially his later works, where he specifically acknowledges military resources having the ability to generate attraction if used for protection and assistance.
As such, the article draws upon these concepts and theories to establish defensive systems as a hybrid resource that is hard in form, but capable of producing soft power effects, and in the Israel-UAE case, become instruments of normalization.
However, another argument put forth by the article concerns the limitations of soft power being used in such a manner.
Nye argues that such resources do not automatically translate to desired outcomes, and in this case, it raises a potent paradox – while defensive systems can generate desired soft power diplomacy, it mainly operates at the level of governments and security organizations, and does not always extend to the wider public, or other states, or eliminates political questions that defines how the region views the provider, which, in this case, is Israel.

Defensive technology as diplomacy
The literature on arms transfers as a diplomatic instrument is well established.
However, nowhere is it more pronounced than in the case of Israel, which, facing growing diplomatic isolation ever since its formation, used arms sales to build relationships with governments that were otherwise reluctant to engage with it openly.
Using arms sales as means of pursuing its economic and political interests, Israel has transformed itself into a mid-level supplier.
However, what distinguishes the country’s arms sales from purely commercial transactions to ones that has helped it to achieve its political interests, is that it follows three primary logics – strategic, economic, and risk-related.
Defensive technologies used in diplomacy are not merely about export metrics and commercial gains.
They go deeper, creating three levels that justify their diplomatic appeal.
The primary functions of these technologies include intercepting incoming threats, such as missiles, rockets, and drones, mainly to protect the territory rather than projecting force.
This allows them to build relationships with states with which they previously had no diplomatic ties, reinforcing the provider’s image as a ‘problem solver’ or protector of its allies.
Existing classifications of missile-defense cooperation differentiate between sales, cooperative research and development, and hosting a provider’s systems on a partner’s territory.
Building on these studies, the article analyses three levels of defensive cooperation, namely, transfer, co-development, and deployment.

Moving to the first layer, i.e., transfer, the provider sells or supplies a defensive system to another state which is then operated by the recipient state. The relationship here is mainly commercial, with limited political signaling. Above this layer is co-development, wherein the provider and the recipient develop the defensive technology jointly, either directly through state organizations or private defense firms, resulting in the creation of long-term industrial and technological ties between the states along with shared stake in the products. The joint Israel-US co-development of defensive systems such as David’s Sling and the Arrow can be cited as examples. The third level is deployment, wherein the provider sends its own systems and personnel to defend the recipient’s territory, especially during an active crisis. As a result, the provider’s forces become directly involved in the recipient’s security. Each level increases three things, namely, the depth of operational integration between states, the visibility of the relationship, and the cost and risk borne by the provider. When the provider is so fully engaged in the relationship, it also strengthens political ties. Each sale signals a willingness to trade; co-development signals a willingness to share technologies; and deployment signals a willingness to bear risk on the partner’s behalf.
Defensive technologies as a source of attraction
Joseph Nye describes soft power as the ability to shape the preferences of others through attraction rather than coercion or payment, locating its sources in a country’s culture, political values, and foreign policies. In his later works, Nye acknowledged that military resources can also generate attraction when used for protection, assistance, or cooperation. Such a definition opens the door to treating defensive technologies as a potential source of soft power. However, military relationships can also create dependency or resentment rather than attraction. Four conditions must be met to ensure defensive technologies generate attraction rather than the previous conditions.
The first condition is benign purpose. Under this condition, unlike offensive technologies, defensive systems can be framed as protective rather than threatening. Let’s take the example of a missile interceptor, like the Israeli Iron Dome System. When this system is deployed over an ally’s city, it is not considered as an act of war or striking anyone since its deployment is framed as protecting the critical infrastructure of the ally from incoming missile threats during active conflict situations. Here, the distinction is primarily based on the intent of the provider. If defensive weapons can be distinguished from the offensive ones, it becomes easier for states to secure themselves without resorting to threatening others, thereby easing the security dilemma issue. Yet, such a framing is not universal. This is because adversaries may consider missile defense systems, irrespective of the intent, as hostile since it weakens their ability to deter or retaliate, particularly in the Gulf where Iran is likely to view Israeli air defense systems as anything but benign. However, irrespective of the threat, for the recipient state, protective or defensive technologies are much easier to accept than offensive ones since it carries less moral and political baggage that are often associated with arms sales, many of which have been prone to criticisms, especially in situations when they are used to commit human rights violations.
Another condition is visible beneficiaries. Air defense outputs are observable, i.e., interceptors can be seen, reported, or counted, and they primarily aim to protect the recipient state’s people and civilian infrastructure. In the case of the UAE, Israeli officials have publicly reported that its systems have intercepted dozens of Iranian missiles, with the US Ambassador crediting the deployment to Israel-UAE’s growing diplomatic relationship made possible via the Abraham Accords. Visibility matters because soft power depends on how audiences perceive and interpret actions, not only on a state’s resources. This gives tangible value to systems that many forms of security cooperation cannot, and it allows the contributions of the provider to be recognized publicly. US’ highly publicized relief efforts following the 2004 tsunami is one such example, leading to favorable views of the US in Indonesia that rose from 15% to 38% by 2005.
A third condition is costliness and credibility. The promise, or credibility of commitment or support, is more believable when the party making it is ready to bear the rising costs. This is known as “sinking costs.” Paying a price up front shows the commitment is genuine, since a state that did not value the relationship would not pay to keep it. This distinction separates the levels of defensive cooperation. If the sale were purely commercial, the recipient would pay, the provider would earn profits, and the sale would reveal little about how much the relationship matters to the provider. However, deployment, especially during a crisis, reverses this dynamic. The provider is willing to give up resources and accept risks on behalf of the partner, as the upcoming section will show how Israel’s 2026 deployment differed from its previous sales. articles.title: Zelenskyy warns Trump sanctions waiver risks fueling Russian aggression
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to waive impending sanctions and tariffs on Russia would hand Moscow an economic...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to waive impending sanctions and tariffs on Russia would hand Moscow an economic reprieve and risk emboldening further Russian aggression.
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians."
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related U.S. sanctions and tariffs - including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas - that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelenskyy said Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin and encourages more attacks by Russia.
"It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people," wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia on Friday struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites. "This certainly does not stop the war."
The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. "Is Russia preparing for this? I think so," Zelenskyy wrote.
Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Friday called the Trump waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before U.S. midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the U.S. from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate."
U.S. Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement on Friday.
Graham, who died in July, strongly supported U.S. assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope that there would be continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented the late senator's absence.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," Zelenskyy posted on Saturday.
The Ukrainian leader predicted that the U.S. under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday's waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month.
"I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," Zelenskyy wrote.

articles.title: Moscow welcomes Trump’s sanctions waiver as Ukraine voices alarm
articles.summary: Russia on Saturday welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions targeting Moscow, calling it a historic move as Ukraine warned that easing economic pressu...
articles.full_text:
Russia on Saturday welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions targeting Moscow, calling it a historic move as Ukraine warned that easing economic pressure would encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to continue the war.
Trump signed an executive order Friday suspending the application of sanctions provisions under the Lindsey Graham Act, a law designed to increase pressure on Russia’s energy and defense sectors, its officials and the network of tankers Moscow uses to circumvent Western restrictions.
The decision comes as Russian forces intensify attacks on Ukrainian cities and diplomatic efforts led by Washington remain deadlocked, raising concerns among Kyiv and its European allies that the Trump administration is easing pressure on Moscow without securing meaningful concessions.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, praised the decision on social media, describing the suspension of the law as an “important and truly historic moment.”
Dmitriev argued that the sanctions would have caused serious damage to the U.S. economy and global markets. The Kremlin and Putin had not publicly commented on the decision as of Saturday.
The waiver followed an arrangement between Trump and Putin under which Moscow agreed to release substantial quantities of diesel onto global markets amid mounting pressure on fuel prices. Trump’s decision to suspend the new measures marks a diplomatic gain for Russia as Washington struggles to broker an end to the war.
The Graham Act, named after the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, was designed to tighten restrictions on Russia’s energy and defense industries, officials linked to Putin and its so-called shadow fleet of tankers. It also included provisions targeting countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas.
Trump’s order suspends the application of the new measures under a national-interest waiver. It does not automatically remove sanctions imposed on Russia under earlier U.S. measures.
The decision has intensified concerns in Kyiv that Washington could weaken its leverage over Moscow while Russian forces continue their offensive.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the waiver Saturday, arguing that easing sanctions would reward Russia despite its continued attacks.
“A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin, all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy said on social media, urging Ukraine’s allies to maintain pressure on Moscow.
The sanctions decision came as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukraine, including repeated strikes on the capital, Kyiv, as the war enters its fifth year.
Russian forces struck the southern city of Kherson on Saturday, killing one person and wounding 22, local officials said. The attack underscored the continuing toll of the war even as Washington pursues negotiations.
The conflict, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. Russian forces occupy large areas of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has repeatedly vowed to seize the remaining territory Moscow claims in eastern Ukraine.
Speaking to military leaders Friday while wearing military uniform, Putin said he saw a positive trend in the operations of Russian forces and reiterated that capturing the rest of the Donetsk region remained a major objective.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” Putin said, using the Kremlin’s term for the Ukrainian region.
Russian strikes have intensified in recent weeks, putting additional pressure on Ukrainian air defenses as the country prepares for another winter of war. Kyiv has struggled to intercept incoming missiles and drones while seeking additional defensive systems from its allies.
Putin’s remarks signaled that Moscow intends to continue its military campaign despite diplomatic efforts to secure a ceasefire.
European leaders responded to the growing uncertainty over Washington’s approach by reaffirming their support for Ukraine and calling for continued economic pressure on Russia.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday during a European Union summit, seeking sustained financial and military assistance as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated.
European Council President António Costa warned against easing pressure on Moscow while Russian forces continued their attacks.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
European leaders have argued that maintaining sanctions and strengthening Ukraine’s defenses are necessary to persuade Russia to accept a meaningful ceasefire and negotiate an end to the war.
The EU has also signaled that it intends to maintain its restrictions on Moscow while preparing further measures.
Zelenskyy has sought additional air defense systems, support for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and continued funding to sustain the country’s defense effort. His appeal came as European governments weighed how to maintain assistance amid uncertainty over the future direction of U.S. policy.
The European response reflects growing concern that Washington’s willingness to ease sanctions could undermine the pressure intended to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
U.S.-led negotiations have yet to produce a breakthrough, with disputes over territory, security guarantees and the terms of a possible ceasefire continuing to obstruct progress.
Trump has expressed frustration with both Putin and Zelenskyy over the lack of progress toward ending the conflict. His increasingly strained relationship with the Ukrainian leader has added to concerns in Kyiv that Washington could press Ukraine to make concessions while offering Moscow economic relief.
The sanctions waiver has heightened those fears, particularly as Ukraine faces intensified Russian bombardments and questions over the reliability of some U.S.-provided military and intelligence support.
For Ukraine, the immediate concern is that easing economic pressure could give Russia greater room to sustain its military campaign. For European governments, the decision raises questions about how to maintain a unified strategy if Washington takes a more conciliatory approach toward Moscow.
Russia’s public celebration of the waiver reflects the potential diplomatic value of the move for Putin, even as the Kremlin continues to pursue its territorial objectives by force.

Yemeni media spokesman Fayyad al-Noman said government forces killed Brigadier General Abdulrahman Mohammed Sufyan Wajih al-Din near Mount Han in Taiz, identifying the Houthi commander as director of Dhi al-Sufal.
Senior commander slain
Yemeni media spokesman Fayyad al-Noman said on Friday that government forces had killed Brigadier General Abdulrahman Mohammed Sufyan Wajih al-Din, also known as Abu al-Karrar, during intense clashes near Mount Han in the southwestern city of Taiz, according to Anadolu Agency. Al-Noman announced the death on the social media platform X, identifying the slain officer as director of Dhi al-Sufal in Ibb province and a senior figure in the Houthi military structure.
Front line flashpoint
Officials did not specify when the clash occurred or provide further details on the circumstances of the killing, and there was no immediate comment from Houthi authorities regarding the incident. Taiz has remained a major flashpoint in Yemen's war, with government troops and Houthi fighters engaged in repeated battles for control of the strategic southwestern city and its surrounding highlands.
Protracted conflict
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized government. Fighting has continued around key cities including Taiz despite repeated diplomatic efforts to broker a lasting ceasefire, leaving the region locked in a protracted stalemate.

Yemen's foreign minister is blasting Iran's offer to mediate the war between the internationally recognized government and the Iran-backed Houthi militant group.

The two sides discussed "the latest developments in Palestine and Yemen, emphasizing diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions," according to the Iranian government.
"During the bilateral talks, FM Araghchi also reviewed the latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing diplomatic trends and emphasizing Islamic cooperation to face shared regional challenges," the Iranian government said on X.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened."
"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said.
He added any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorization "if it is requested of us."
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defense."
Yemen's Houthis free 159 pro-government fighters under amnesty
Yemen's Houthis on Saturday announced the release of 159 pro-government fighters under an amnesty announced after they seized swathes of land in a major offensive last month.
The prisoners had "voluntarily surrendered themselves without fighting" as the Iran-backed group captured strategic positions along the Red Sea, Houthi official Abdelqader al-Murtada told a press conference in Sanaa.
The Houthis' war with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government reignited in July after four years of calm, triggering attacks on Saudi oil shipments and other targets including airports.
The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmed the unilateral release of 159 prisoners and said it had given support by organizing interviews and health checks, contacting families and helping arrange transport.
Murtada said 323 prisoners were released under the amnesty last month after surrendering in Hodeidah governorate.
Iran backs "political process" to resolve Saudi-Houthi conflict, foreign minister says

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a major attack one week ago.
"We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad.
Araghchi repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides. Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture.
On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi Arabia accused Tehran of encouraging the group's escalation.
In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option."
The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, which also includes armed groups in Iraq.

articles.title: Iran risks losing ground as East-West trade routes expand - Iran International
articles.summary: Iran risks losing ground as East-West trade routes expand  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Investment in trade routes linking Asia and Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus is putting pressure on Iran’s ambitions to become a major transit hub, with neighboring countries developing transport and digital networks that bypass Iranian territory.
Among them is the Middle Corridor, a network of rail, road and sea links connecting China to Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus while bypassing Iran.
The corridor is intended not only to connect Chinese and European markets. Countries along the route are also expanding trade among themselves, and the broader connectivity push extends beyond cargo to energy, information technology and data.
On October 15, the presidents of Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan inaugurated a 380-kilometer fiber-optic link across the Caspian seabed with a capacity of more than 400 terabits per second. Part of the Digital Silk Way initiative, the cable complements the Middle Corridor.
Beyond carrying data along the East-West axis, its backers say it will help attract investment in AI data centers, cloud services and high-tech industries.
In its latest report, the World Bank projects that, if the planned investments materialize, freight volumes across the Caspian could rise from 8.8 million tons in 2023 to 32.1 million tons in 2040.
The report also finds that developing the corridor could, in the long term, increase the combined GDP of host countries by about 3.3 percent, equivalent to approximately $58 billion at current levels of economic activity, and raise employment by 2.9 percent.
These gains depend on policy and operational reforms alongside construction. The World Bank identifies at least $25 billion in infrastructure investment needs through 2040, plus an estimated $30 billion for connecting infrastructure, logistics facilities and equipment.
One of the most contentious proposed links is the route through southern Armenia that would connect mainland Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave, known in Azerbaijan as the Zangezur corridor.
Under agreements reached since August 2025, the US-backed project is being developed as the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP, with Armenia retaining sovereignty and jurisdiction over its territory.
Azerbaijan projects that the route could carry 15 million tons of freight annually. The section through Armenia is roughly 42 to 43 kilometers long.
After several years of fierce opposition to the proposed Zangezur corridor, Iran appears to be taking a more pragmatic approach to Armenia’s inclusion in East-West transport networks, although concerns over American involvement remain.
Iran’s ambassador in Yerevan expressed concern in September about an American presence near the border and proposed a mechanism to address Tehran’s concerns. On October 16, Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said Iran had asked about the possible deployment of US military forces on Armenian territory and that Yerevan had assured Tehran this would not happen. He said he believed the Iranian side was satisfied with Armenia’s answers.
The World Bank estimates that developing the Middle Corridor could increase Armenia’s GDP by 3.4 percent, equivalent to $873 million, and raise employment by 3.9 percent in the long term. Armenia, however, is not yet a transit country on the route; the report assumes a direct rail link through the country becomes operational in the early 2030s.
Iran’s transit ambitions face growing competition
Azerbaijan and Iran have also pursued an alternative connection between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan through Iranian territory, known as the Aras corridor.
That route could preserve a role for Iran in regional transit, but participation in one connecting segment would fall short of Tehran’s broader ambition to become a central hub for trade between Asia and Europe. Western sanctions also complicate efforts to attract European businesses to routes through Iran.
A comparison with Turkey, a key link between the Middle Corridor and European markets, is telling. The World Bank estimates that corridor development could increase Turkey’s GDP by more than $47 billion and employment by about 4.4 percent in the long term.
Iran also faces competition from other regional transport plans. Iraq, with participation from Qatar, the UAE and Turkey, is advancing the Development Road, intended to link the Grand Faw port to the Turkish border at an estimated cost of about $17 billion. Iraqi officials have projected annual revenues of roughly $4 billion, although the project’s returns depend on financing, completion and demand.
The proposed India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor and Syria’s Four Seas initiative, linking the Mediterranean, Persian Gulf, Black Sea and Caspian region, likewise reflect efforts to develop alternative networks. These projects remain at different stages of development, and their commercial success is not assured.
More than two decades after Iran, India and Russia agreed to establish the International North-South Transport Corridor, Tehran’s ambition to become a transit hub linking India with Russia and European markets remains only partly realized. Shipments have moved through Iran, but the existence of traffic alone does not demonstrate that the route has fulfilled its wider commercial promise.
Iran’s weak logistics performance adds to the challenge. In the World Bank’s 2023 Logistics Performance Index, it ranked 123rd with a score of 2.3 out of five. Geography gives Iran potential advantages, but converting them into sustained transit business requires reliable infrastructure, efficient border procedures and commercially viable international connections.

articles.title: US envoy urges Israel to punish settler terrorism against journalist

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Saturday condemned an attack by illegal Israeli settlers on a female Washington Post photographer as an "act of terror," demanding that Israeli authorities prosecute and imprison those responsible.
"Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards," Huckabee wrote on X, taking a far stronger tone than an earlier statement from Washington.
Clad in black and their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on Friday on a village's harvest in the Israeli-occupied West Bank that injured at least two people, including Heidi Levine.
Netanyahu's main rival in the elections, Gadi Eisenkot also called it "Jewish terror" - the same term Levine used when speaking to The Associated Press on Saturday from her hospital bed.
"I've been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today," Levine said, adding that she was "shocked and insulted" that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as an alleged one.
Netanyahu in the past has attributed the violence to a small number of troublemakers. But cars have been burned, trees damaged and people hurt in communities across the Palestinian territory, with some people calling this the most dangerous season yet.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law, a position upheld by the United Nations and widely supported by the international community. Many have expanded into sprawling residential communities, while illegal Israeli settlers have established hundreds of additional outposts without official authorization, often benefiting from Israeli military protection.
Israel occupied the West Bank, Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. Palestinians seek these territories for an independent state, but the West Bank remains under Israeli military occupation as settlement expansion continues.
International condemnation of Israel's settlement policies has intensified, with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi becoming one of the latest senior officials to demand action. During talks with Israeli President Isaac Herzog this week, Wang urged Israel to halt and reverse its forced settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, according to a spokesperson Friday.
