articles.title: Israeli settler terrorists attack European delegation in West Bank
articles.summary: Illegal Israeli settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation visiting the occupied West Bank on Saturday, injuring several people as representatives from France, Belgium and...
articles.full_text:
Illegal Israeli settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation visiting the occupied West Bank on Saturday, injuring several people as representatives from France, Belgium and Poland toured the Palestinian town of Taybeh.
The attack took place after an official ceremony marking the signing of a twinning agreement between the Palestinian town of Taybeh and the French town of Saint-Pierre, Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khourieh told Anadolu Agency (AA).
The ceremony was attended by the French and Belgian consuls, a Polish representative whose name was not disclosed, and Saint-Pierre Mayor Christian Ravain.
The attack targeted the delegation in the western part of the town, as well as Palestinians who were picking olives.
It left several town residents injured and shattered the window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian delegation, Khourieh added.
The 78-year-old French mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.
"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.
"The whole world needs to know what's happening," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."
Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack, but he did not need hospital care.
He, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.
He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.
Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians' annual harvest after months of escalating attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must "urgently halt criminal violence" and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, with his Belgian counterpart issuing a similar call.
Israeli Army Radio, citing witnesses and footage, also said that the occupiers hurled stones at one of the diplomatic vehicles, smashing its window.
Footage showed a member of the delegation lying on the ground after the attack. The person shown lying on the ground beside the diplomatic vehicle was Bernard Boudot, a French politician and mayor of Aulnoy-lez-Valenciennes in northern France, the broadcaster said.
Israel’s Channel 12, citing the Israeli military, reported that the incident was "under review” and none had been arrested immediately.
Khourieh described the attack as "a flagrant violation of the sanctity of diplomatic and humanitarian work” and part of ongoing restrictions imposed on Palestinian farmers.
Attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians and their land have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began in early October and provides a key source of income for thousands of Palestinian families.
Israel's foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to shore up support from the fiercely pro-settlement far-right in the October 27 election, instead alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.
Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.
"We urge caution before drawing conclusions" about the attacks, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
His main rival in the elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was "burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses".
The attacks are "Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government", Eisenkot said.

articles.title: Israeli settlers burn olive trees, attack 8 farmers in West Bank
articles.summary: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank on Friday, burning olive trees, throwing stones and injuring residents and an American photojournalis...
articles.full_text:
Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank on Friday, burning olive trees, throwing stones and injuring residents and an American photojournalist as violence escalated during the annual harvest season.
About 80 settlers dressed in black descended on a terraced olive grove above the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, where Palestinian residents had gathered to pick olives, according to Reuters witnesses. Some carried gas canisters, while others used slingshots to hurl stones at the farmers.
The villagers retreated down the hillside before some threw stones back at the attackers. Olive harvesting is an important annual tradition for Palestinian families and a vital source of income for many farming communities.
“The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the assault.
At least two Israeli military jeeps later sped through the area as villagers moved out of their path. Soldiers fired tear gas toward Palestinians, while the sound of live gunfire echoed across the area. A Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun.
The Israeli military said soldiers and border police officers deployed to the scene fired warning shots. It also acknowledged that troops fired toward a person they believed posed a threat.
“Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable,” the military said, adding that attempts to provoke tensions between communities undermined security.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the incident was under investigation.
Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post, was among those injured in Abu Falah. Palestinian medics said at least two people were taken to hospitals in the Ramallah area.
Video of the attack showed Levine lying on a dirt path with her hands covering her face as at least three settlers stood around her.
Speaking from a hospital bed, Levine said the attackers pushed her to the ground and repeatedly kicked her.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me,” she said.
Levine said her Palestinian colleagues intervened before medics transported her by ambulance to a clinic in Abu Falah and then to a hospital in Ramallah.
The Washington Post later reported that she had suffered lacerations across her body and a broken rib. She also required surgery on one hand after a finger was torn open, exposing bone.
Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor, condemned the attack and called for a thorough investigation.
“This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said.
He said Levine had been wearing visible markings identifying her as a journalist and urged authorities to investigate the assault and ensure accountability.
The U.S. State Department said it was deeply concerned about the harm suffered by an American citizen overseas and had contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance.
The department also condemned criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and supported holding those responsible accountable.
The assault in Abu Falah was part of a wider wave of settler violence reported across the occupied West Bank as Palestinians began their annual olive harvest.
Local officials and the Palestine Red Crescent Society reported attacks in at least eight villages in the northern West Bank, where many of the territory's olive groves are concentrated.
The Red Crescent said its medics had treated 14 injured people, while local officials reported at least four injuries.
Palestinian officials said at least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest season began earlier in October. They also reported damage to thousands of olive trees.
In Turmus Ayya, another village near Ramallah, settlers attacked farmers harvesting olives and burned three cars, according to local accounts.
Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack, said the assailants approached the farmers before targeting someone who was alone.
“They snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him,” he said.
Yesh Din, an Israeli organization that monitors settlement activity and settler violence, reported at least 170 attacks against Palestinians since Sept. 27, around the beginning of the olive harvest.
The organization’s figures highlight the risks facing Palestinian farmers during a season that is central to their livelihoods and cultural traditions. Attacks on farmers, damage to trees and restrictions on access to groves can threaten both current harvests and future income.
Residents and rights groups have accused Israeli authorities of failing to adequately prevent the assaults or hold perpetrators accountable. Settler violence has intensified this year, with a further increase reported in the weeks leading up to Israel's Oct. 27 election.
Netanyahu has criticized settler violence, but his government has faced international criticism over its response. His right-wing coalition has overseen an expansion of Israeli settlements and smaller outposts across the West Bank.
The attacks have also drawn condemnation from some of Israel's longtime allies, including Britain, which has considered sanctions over settler violence.
About 500,000 Israeli settlers live alongside at least 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank. The United Nations and most countries consider Israeli settlements in the territory illegal under international law. Israel disputes that position and regards the territory as disputed rather than occupied.

articles.title: Euronews crew say they were encircled and robbed covering protests - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Euronews crew say they were encircled and robbed covering protests  Euronews.comFrance: violence against journalists during protests requires immediate sanctions and implementation of our post-mission recommendations  European Federation of Journalists
articles.full_text:
Euronews correspondents in Paris covering the protests reported being targeted by masked individuals on Saturday’s major nationwide demonstrations following calls on social media to target media outlets and professionals to prevent coverage.
Euronews’ crew was assaulted by looters and rioters in Paris near the Place de la Republique on Saturday as they were covering the ongoing joint major protests organised by the so-called ‘Yellow Vests’ and student-led groups.
The crew was headed to another location from Place de la Republique – where the protests were being staged.
Shortly into their journey, they were confronted by masked looters robbing the nearby Intermarché Express supermarket on 14 Place Jacques Bonsergent, which diverges from Place de la Republique, and filmed it.
“We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us,” said Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris.
“They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing a gas mask, protective eyewear and a helmet, he was not seriously harmed."
"He managed to get away with just some bruises on his face," she added.
Our correspondent also noted that the looters stole their camera during the scuffles, which was eventually brought back by a group of youngsters who saw what was happening. The returned camera however did not have the SD card, and all footage recorded was lost.
Nilsson-Julien reported seeing things on fire in the area in the immediate vicinity of the supermarket, and loud police sirens.
“It is to be honest anarchy in the streets. There are many young people who seem like they are ready for a fight and looting going on. So, the calm protests of earlier today, at least in this area, are completely over,” she said.
Another Euronews correspondent, Valerie Gauriat, covering the protests at the Place de la Republique also reported a violent incident with a masked individual earlier while conducting an interview with a protester.
She noted that a protester slapped the back of her head and mumbled profane words as they walked past, denouncing media presence at the demonstrations.
The incidents come after certain groups on social media called on protesters to target media outlets and personnel, to prevent “the spread of misinformation” about the protests and reported violence.

articles.title: Alberta, home to the world’s 4th-largest oil reserves, will vote on a first step to leaving Canada - Fortune
articles.summary: Alberta, home to the world’s 4th-largest oil reserves, will vote on a first step to leaving Canada  FortuneA Calgary Crowd Rallies for Canada as Alberta’s Vote on Secession Nears  The New York TimesAlberta referendum expected to bring finality, but also more questions on separation  Global NewsIndependence supporters rally outside Alberta's legislature Saturday  CBCAlberta Support for Canada Rises Ahead of Separation Referendum  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
For decades, Alberta separatism was a fringe cause. On Monday, voters in Canada’s oil heartland will decide whether to take the first step toward a referendum on leaving the country.
Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is not voting to leave Canada on Oct. 19. Instead, voters will decide whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said that support for starting the separation process, which was around 23% in a recent poll, is “still too high for my liking.”
Alberta has long feuded with the federal government over oil and federal power. Liberal prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and, decades later, his son Justin became deeply unpopular in the province over energy policy.
Justin Trudeau’s government imposed a national carbon tax and other climate measures that Alberta leaders said hurt its oil industry. Yet separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said.
Then came the pandemic and the Freedom Convoy, which paralyzed parts of Ottawa, the Canadian capital, and blocked major Canada-U.S. border crossings.
“They needed a new cause,” Kenney told The Associated Press. “And it naturally morphed into separatism.”
Pandemic-era restrictions supercharged separatism
Jeff Rath, a leader of the independence movement, said federal vaccine rules preventing unvaccinated Canadians from flying were his breaking point.
“If Trudeau won’t let me leave Alberta, I’m just going to pick up my whole province and go,” Rath recalled telling a friend. “COVID was really the straw that broke the camel’s back.”
“A lot of people were radicalized by the convoy,” he said.
The 2022 Freedom Convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a broader revolt against pandemic restrictions.
Kenney said people mobilized over anger at globalization, vaccines and pandemic restrictions, while social media allowed previously isolated activists to find one another and organize.
“They found each other and they found a cause,” Kenney said.
Kenney said the movement also became more professional, building organizations, raising money and drawing in political operatives with campaign and fundraising experience.
He also sees substantial overlap between separatist activists and people who support Russian President Vladimir Putin or believe conspiracy theories about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kenney stressed he was describing activists, not typical separation voters, whom he characterized as frustrated Albertans sending Ottawa a message.
Kenney said the MAGA movement has been “inspirational” for some separatist activists. He said they “tried to infiltrate with at least some success” the United Conservative Party he founded. Smith replaced Kenney in 2022 after appealing to United Conservative Party members angry over COVID-19 restrictions.
“Literally, you can look at the players,” Kenney said of the convoy and separatist movements. “It’s the same people.”
Carney finds unusual support in Alberta
Prime Minister Mark Carney has made getting Alberta oil to new markets a national priority and backs a proposed pipeline to the West Coast. His more business- and energy-friendly policies, along with his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and 51st-state rhetoric, have made the federal Liberal leader unusually popular in conservative Alberta.
Kenney, one of the most prominent conservative critics of Trudeau’s approach to Alberta, said Carney “speaks as an Albertan,” understands the province’s grievances and aspirations, and is moving in the right direction on energy.
Rath called Carney a “formidable opponent,” saying “every major politician” in Alberta and Canada is against the separatists and acknowledged an uphill battle. He said he would be “thrilled” with more than 30% of the vote — well short of a majority.
“Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life,” Carney said. “We have to be strong and we are stronger together.”
Activists go to Washington
Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States, and separatists have taken their campaign directly to Washington.
Rath confirmed he and other independence advocates met with U.S. State Department officials three times and presented a document outlining what an independent Alberta could offer the United States.
Rath claimed people involved in the meetings were going directly to the White House and that a possible oil pipeline through the U.S. to the Pacific was “literally a topic of our last meeting with the U.S. State Department.”
The State Department said that “The Department regularly meets with a wide range of representatives. The vote is a decision for the people of Alberta.”
Kenney called the outreach “bonkers,” saying people with “zero democratic mandate” were discussing with a foreign government “the status of a separate state that does not exist.”
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta “a natural partner.”
Future of separatism
Keith Wilson, another Alberta independence leader who was lead counsel for the 2022 convoy organizers, said separatists see the vote as a way to give Alberta more leverage in dealing with Ottawa, even short of independence.
“That’s right, because it’s called leverage. It’s called negotiation,” Wilson said. He said he would accept substantial structural changes to Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa short of independence.
“I don’t think it will recede,” Kenney said of the separatist movement in Alberta. Even 10% to 20% support, he noted, would far exceed separatists’ historic vote share. If low turnout pushed them toward 30%, “they’re going to be even more emboldened.”
“That’s not a threat to Canada,” Kenney said. “But it is a threat to the conservative movement.”
Alberta is not Canada’s only national-unity challenge. Quebec voters returned the separatist Parti Quebecois to power Oct. 5, although support for independence remains around 30% and its leader has said he will not hold a referendum while Trump is U.S. president.
Quebec voters have twice rejected independence, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.

articles.title: Egypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked - The Straits Times

CAIRO, Oct 17 - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced an emergency session on Sunday.
"It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defence.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.
Sisi said Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited, to discuss issues including security and navigation in the Red Sea.
"I know this requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that authorisation if we are asked," Sisi said.
Shortly after he spoke, parliament said it would hold a plenary session at 1 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Sunday in response to the request, though it did not disclose the agenda.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist president Mohamed Morsi in 2013.

Saudi FDI Net Inflows Rise 33.5% in FY2025 to SAR159 Billion
Saudi Arabia recorded foreign direct investment net inflows of SAR159 billion, equivalent to $41.7 billion, in fiscal year 2025, an increase of 33.5% compared with the prior year, according to SPA. The same report indicated that the kingdom's FDI stock climbed 8.3% to reach SAR1.06 trillion, or $278 billion.
The figures point to sustained expansion in foreign direct investment over recent years. In 2025, inflows stood at five times their 2017 level, while the FDI stock doubled across the same period, the report stated.
Between 2017 and 2025, FDI inflows expanded at a compound annual rate of 24%, and the FDI stock grew at 10%, reflecting continued growth in foreign investment and a larger accumulated FDI base in the kingdom.
The report attributed the trend to Saudi Arabia's growing appeal among foreign investors and rising confidence in the Saudi economy and its outlook, supported by economic and structural changes introduced since the launch of Saudi Vision 2030.
The results were presented as evidence of progress in strengthening the kingdom's position as an attractive investment destination, consistent with Vision 2030 objectives to diversify the economy and raise FDI levels.
Saudi Arabia continues to improve its investment environment, expand domestic investment, and attract high-quality foreign investment, the report added.

EU-GCC: Energy security, diversification of sources cornerstone of economic stability and sustainable development
- The joint EU-GCC statement highlights energy security and diversification of energy sources as essential for economic stability and sustainable development
- Participants called for stronger Gulf-European cooperation to ensure reliable and sustainable energy supplies
RIYADH: A joint European-Gulf statement emphasized the importance of energy security and diversifying energy sources in consolidating economic stability and supporting sustainable development paths, calling for strengthening Gulf-European cooperation to ensure the reliability and sustainability of energy supplies, developing infrastructure and interconnection, and expanding partnerships in modern technologies of common interest.
The joint statement issued today in Brussels by the second conference of heads of legislative councils of the European Parliament and the Gulf Cooperation Council stressed that energy security represents a common strategic interest between the two sides, in light of the challenges facing energy markets and the disruptions affecting their supplies, and the repercussions they impose on economic sectors, especially industry, as well as their impact on societies and living standards.
The participants called on the upcoming summit between the Gulf Cooperation Council and the European Union to give greater political momentum to cooperation in the field of energy, and to explore opportunities to provide reliable, diversified and sustainable supplies, thereby enhancing long-term energy security and supporting mutual interests.
Maritime coordination to protect shipping lanes and energy supplies
In a related context, the participants welcomed calls to strengthen Operation Aspidis of the European Union Naval Force, and encouraged closer coordination between the Saudi-led multinational maritime defense alliance and EU operations within the framework of the Common Security and Defence Policy, in order to protect common maritime routes and ensure the flow of energy supplies.
The statement expressed concern about developments in the Red Sea and the threat they pose to this vital corridor linking Europe and Asia, praising the contributions of the EU Naval Force’s Operations Aspidis and Atalanta.
The participants stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation in maritime security, protecting critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity, as well as combating terrorism, preventing violent extremism, and enhancing civil protection and resilience, while emphasizing the need to respect freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al-Mandab.
Navigation disruptions reinforce the importance of Gulf-European connectivity.
The statement noted that the disruptions to shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, which it attributed to Iranian attacks and attacks by its proxies, highlighted the close link between the security and prosperity of the Arabian Gulf and Europe, and the need to strengthen maritime, land, air and digital connectivity networks to serve trade, energy, investment and security.
The participants called for developing the strategic partnership between the two sides and enhancing its ability to cope with crises, through a secure and sustainable infrastructure, more resilient supply chains, and a stable and predictable economic framework, in order to support common interests and enhance resilience to regional and international turmoil.
They also urged the upcoming summit to give a clear political signal to resume negotiations on a comprehensive free trade agreement between the GCC and the EU, which would enhance trade and investment relations and broaden the prospects for economic cooperation.
Condemnation of Iranian attacks and emphasis on regional security
On the security front, the participants condemned the Iranian missile and drone attacks against the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, whether carried out directly or through proxies, including the targeting of civilian, economic, and vital facilities, airports, service facilities, and infrastructure.
They expressed their solidarity with the GCC countries and their peoples, affirming the right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, and calling on Iran and its proxies to immediately and unconditionally cease attacks and comply with Security Council Resolution 2817 of 2026.
The statement stressed that dialogue, diplomacy and international law are the basis for restoring stability and reaching lasting solutions that address regional threats, in a way that preserves the security of the region and safeguards freedom of navigation in vital sea lanes.
A strategic partnership that goes beyond energy and security
The statement came at the conclusion of the second conference of the heads of legislative councils of the European Parliament and the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf, which was held in Brussels with the participation of the President of the European Parliament and the heads of legislative councils of the member states of the Cooperation Council, as a continuation of the outcomes of the meeting held in Abu Dhabi on June 23, 2025, and building on the results of the first summit between the two sides in Brussels on October 16, 2024.
The participants stressed the importance of developing the Gulf-European partnership towards deeper strategic cooperation that includes a parliamentary dimension, in addition to enhancing communication between peoples, cultural, educational and tourism exchange, and moving towards mutually beneficial arrangements for visa-free travel with the remaining five GCC countries.
The statement reflects a trend towards linking energy security with the stability of maritime routes, the resilience of supply chains, and economic integration, making Gulf-European cooperation in these areas a pillar for enhancing regional stability and supporting long-term sustainable development.

articles.full_text:
Do any of these Israeli candidates support a Palestinian state?
On September 26, five leading members of Israel’s self-styled Zionist opposition signed a non-aggression pact, seeking to oust incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 election.
Gathered at the Tel Aviv home of opposition leader Yair Lapid were his co-runner, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of Beyachad; former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the new Yashar party; Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party; and Avigdor Liberman, head of the Yisrael Beiteinu party.
In the statement of principles published after the hours-long meeting, the leaders said, “Despite ideological differences among us, the formation of a Zionist, statesmanlike government dedicated to repair and reconstruction is our shared overarching goal.”
However, how long that pact might last — Liberman has already accused frontrunner Eisenkot of seeking a deal with Netanyahu — how meaningful a change in substance as well as style they offer, and which of them might lead a future coalition, remain open to question.
With the exception of Golan, all take a fundamentally right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges.
None is committed to establishing a Palestinian state, with only the Democrats acknowledging it as a distant, unspecified goal. None, Golan included, accepts that Israel’s war on Gaza amounts to genocide or that it has committed war crimes in killing more than 74,000 people there. Nor has any questioned Israeli military actions against Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Qatar and Iran, instead reserving criticism mostly for how those actions have allowed Israel to be perceived internationally.
“The dominant forces in the opposition such as Bennett, Liberman or Eisenkot represent right-wing politics,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “They are not willing to touch the real, fundamental issue which is at the heart of everything: the Palestinian issue, and the Palestinian aspirations for independence.” He likened them to Netanyahu, but without the corruption allegations and support of far-right figures, such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “Israel as a whole is a right-wing nation,” he added.
So, who are the main opposition figures and what do their parties stand for?
Gadi Eisenkot – Yashar
Credited with originating the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2008, involving “disproportionate force” and large-scale destruction of civilian infrastructure against groups such as Hezbollah and Hamas, Eisenkot served as Israeli military chief from 2015 to 2019.
The 66-year-old entered politics in 2022 with former Defence Minister Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance and later joined the war cabinet assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. In December that year, his son Gal, 25, and two nephews were killed while participating in the genocide in Gaza, losses commentators say have helped forge a connection with an electorate that has come to see itself as scarred by war.
In June 2024, he quit the war cabinet alongside Gantz, accusing Netanyahu of lacking a strategy to end the war. A year later, Eisenkot founded the centrist Yashar (Straight/Honest), advocating for professional government, military service for all – including ultra-Orthodox Jews – and a state commission of inquiry into the failings before October 7.
While notoriously ambiguous on many of Israel’s foreign policy positions, he has been critical of the government’s reliance upon the United States in achieving its war aims, while not questioning those aims themselves. In June, he characterised Washington’s mediated negotiations with Tehran to end the war against Iran that Washington had embarked upon with Israel as “a deal taking shape far from here and far from Israeli interests” and, the same month, railed against US restrictions on Israel’s freedom of action in Lebanon.
Eisenkot has ruled out including the United Arab List, or Ra’am party, in a post-election coalition. In a September 26 Channel 12 interview, he said no Arab party would accept his conditions, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state.
Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid – Beyachad
Beyachad (Together) is the joint list announced in April 2026 by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who served for a combined 18 months in 2021-2022 between Netanyahu governments.
Bennett, a 54-year-old longtime supporter of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, leads the list, with Lapid, the 62-year-old founder of the centrist Yesh Atid party, in second place.
Lapid has called his partner “a right-wing politician, but an honest one”. Neither has prioritised resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or supported a Palestinian state. Though their 2021 coalition included Ra’am, Bennett has acknowledged that this broke an electoral promise.
Lapid has been one of Israel’s most outspoken critics of how its genocide and multiple strikes upon its neighbours are perceived internationally, while rarely questioning the rationale behind those actions. Bennett, in contrast, is more outspoken in his hawkish views. A full-throated supporter of the country’s war on Iran, he also congratulated Israel’s military and security services for a September 2025 attack on Qatar’s capital, Doha, that targeted senior Hamas leaders as they met to consider a Gaza ceasefire proposal put forth by the US. A Qatari security official was killed in the attack, which drew condemnation from across the region and beyond.
They now seek a government composed solely of Zionist parties, also ruling out reliance on Arab parties.
Avigdor Lieberman – Yisrael Beiteinu
The most hawkish voice at Lapid’s table, Lieberman, 68, founded Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) in 1999 to represent right-leaning Russian-speaking immigrants.
Once Netanyahu’s protege, Lieberman has ruled out serving under him or joining a coalition that includes the ultra-Orthodox or relies on Arab parties, which he calls anti-Zionist. He has also rejected a minority government, reportedly making him a principal obstacle to Eisenkot becoming the bloc’s prime ministerial candidate.
In November 2023, Lieberman repeated his 2018 assertion, made then as defence minister, that there were “no innocents in Gaza”. In February, he visited the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom to Israelis, and accused Netanyahu’s government of funding Hamas by allowing the minimal humanitarian aid that has been permitted into Gaza.
The Yisrael Beiteinu leader has been a consistent supporter of Israel’s genocide and subsequent military actions. In September 2025, he joined other Israeli politicians in criticising Netanyahu for the apology to Doha that he had been forced to make by the Trump administration for that month’s strike, saying the apology was instead owed to the Israeli public. Equally, he has argued against any restraint in its invasion of Lebanon, telling the Jerusalem Post in March: “If once again we go for a limited operation, some manoeuvre near the border, maybe talk about a security zone, it’s complete madness.”
“Lieberman does not belong in this bloc,” said Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, an Israeli analyst with Atlas Global Strategies, arguing that his main motivation was hatred of Netanyahu.
However, Ben-Ephraim said, Lieberman “maintains a loyal base and is a crucial force in Israeli politics”. His core constituency is the former Soviet electorate, but he has gained wider trust through his perceived independence.
Observers say he could potentially return to Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc.
Yair Golan – Democrats
The only leader at Lapid’s table from the Zionist left and the only one open to working with Palestinian parties, Golan heads the Democrats, a liberal party that was formed in 2024 through the merger of Labor and the social democratic, secular Meretz.
A retired major-general and former deputy chief of staff, Golan, 64, earned domestic plaudits for driving south during the 2023 Hamas-led attack and helping repel it.
Golan is alone among many in the anti-Netanyahu bloc in his criticism of the government’s war aims, arguing that military achievements are being squandered without a coherent diplomatic and political strategy
In May 2025, two years into the genocide in Gaza, Golan sparked controversy when he told a news conference that a “sane country does not kill babies as a hobby”, accusing ministers of celebrating the starvation of Palestinian children in the territory. He later walked back the comments after widespread criticism in Israel. In October, while praising the achievements of the previous year’s 12-day war against Iran, he told party members that the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at the beginning of the conflict was a “mistake”. “Not because he didn’t deserve to die,” he caveated, “only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel.”
Despite his openness to working with Palestinian parties, in September, Golan backed the disqualification of Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, over an article about October 7, drawing criticism from the Joint List – an alliance of the Arab-led Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties – and commentators.
Roi Zur, a University of Essex specialist in Israeli politics, said that despite Golan and Lieberman’s ideological differences on security and conflict, there will be “no winning coalition without these two”. He added that concerns about a clash between them miss the point, noting that both oppose Netanyahu, favour secularisation and strongly oppose exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.

articles.full_text:
Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly damaged, while restrictions and funding shortages are undermining efforts to prepare for winter, a senior U.N. migration official said late Friday.
Karl Baker, the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response, said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, with each forced move further damaging or destroying tents and other makeshift shelters.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told U.N. News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors and more substantial walls, however, are subject to Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions, which are imposed over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30% of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30% in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organizations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps. Baker warned, however, that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17% of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A cease-fire has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid and shelter supplies have continued.

articles.title: Trump feud with Zelenskyy raises fears over Ukraine aid
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump’s growing dispute with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is raising concerns that Kyiv could lose critical American military and intelligence supp...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s growing dispute with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is raising concerns that Kyiv could lose critical American military and intelligence support as Russia continues its war, with Washington’s efforts to curb fuel prices adding to tensions between the allies.
From threats to restrict intelligence sharing to a potential deal to import Russian diesel, a series of developments has exposed the fragility of the relationship between Kyiv and its most important ally.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelenskyy over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he partly blames for rising energy costs.
The U.S. president has pushed Ukraine to stop targeting Russian energy infrastructure, but Zelenskyy has rejected the demand, arguing that Kyiv cannot halt its attacks while Moscow continues striking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The dispute intensified after disruptions to U.S.-controlled satellite internet services raised concerns about Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly as it prepares for another winter of assaults on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy has responded to Trump with unusually direct public criticism, accusing Washington of increasingly favoring Moscow.
His remarks have fueled fears that the deteriorating relationship could lead to further restrictions on U.S. weapons deliveries, a suspension of battlefield intelligence sharing or additional economic agreements that benefit Russia.
Despite the public confrontation, Kyiv wants to maintain contact with Trump's envoys, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Ukraine is also seeking to preserve its diplomatic relationship with Washington.
Denys Sienik, charge d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said Friday that Kyiv appreciated Trump's efforts to end the war and remained willing to engage in negotiations with Russia.
Trump, meanwhile, said he would continue dealing with both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I want that war to end," Trump told reporters Friday.
Daniel Fried, a former senior State Department official responsible for European affairs from 2005 to 2009, said it remained unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine.
He warned, however, that the fallout was undermining prospects for ending the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskyy has been strained for much of his presidency. In February 2025, Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly reprimanded the Ukrainian leader during a contentious meeting in the Oval Office.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine at various points, while allowing European allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.
Relations had shown signs of stabilizing before Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities became a fresh source of friction this year.
Rising fuel prices have added urgency to the dispute for Trump, whose Republican Party faces a difficult battle to retain its majorities in Congress in November's midterm elections. High gasoline and diesel costs remain a political liability for the administration, analysts say.
But experts attribute much of the increase in energy prices to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which prompted Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure and largely shut the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated with Zelenskyy, Trump turned to Moscow in an effort to increase fuel supplies and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Trump said Oct. 9 that he had reached an agreement with Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
The move raised concerns that Washington could ease economic pressure on Moscow while demanding concessions from Ukraine, potentially giving the Kremlin additional revenue to sustain its war effort.
For Kyiv, the consequences of a breakdown in relations with Washington could be immediate.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital, underscoring concerns about the reliability of intelligence support.
American intelligence has been central to Ukraine's ability to detect incoming Russian missiles and drones, assess battlefield developments and plan military operations. A reduction in that assistance could leave Ukrainian forces less prepared to counter attacks, particularly against power plants and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy system during previous winters, seeking to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall.
Trump has said Washington continues to share intelligence with Kyiv. Zelenskyy, however, told NPR that U.S. officials had warned Ukrainian commanders that intelligence support could be reduced or cut off.
Concerns deepened after Ukraine's Starshield service, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system, was disrupted. Two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said the disruption followed an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported Thursday.
The service has since been partially restored, but the episode highlighted Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by American companies and potentially affected by decisions made by the Trump administration.
Satellite communications are crucial to Ukrainian military coordination, particularly on the front lines. Any prolonged interruption could complicate communications between units and undermine operational effectiveness.
That dependence also gives Trump leverage as he presses Kyiv to pursue negotiations with Moscow.
Trump's approach could face resistance from Republicans in Congress who remain supportive of Ukraine and oppose pressuring Kyiv into a settlement that favors Russia.
Some lawmakers have argued that Washington should maintain support for Ukraine rather than allow Moscow to benefit from a weakening of Western assistance.
Zelenskyy's increasingly forceful responses to Trump carry risks, particularly given Washington's influence over Ukraine's military capabilities. But he may be betting that the balance of power in Congress could shift after the November midterm elections, making it more difficult for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia or further reduce assistance to Kyiv.
That is the assessment of Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration who heads the Global Situation Room consultancy.
Bruen said Zelenskyy understood the risks of confronting Trump but appeared less intimidated by the president's threats than during earlier clashes.
"Zelenskyy knows who he's dealing with," he said. "Trump's threats don't have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office."

articles.title: Merz warns EU irregular migration battle far from over despite drop
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Friday that the European Union still faces significant challenges in managing migration, despite a decline in arrivals and the adoption of n...
articles.full_text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Friday that the European Union still faces significant challenges in managing migration, despite a decline in arrivals and the adoption of new asylum rules aimed at overhauling the bloc's migration system.
"By now almost every head of state and government in the European Union sees it that way: We have a massive problem that places a considerable burden on our societies," Merz said at the EU summit in Brussels.
He said he expressly agreed with this view. "Irregular migration is one of the biggest problems we have in Europe," he added.
Merz commented on the issue on the sidelines of a debate about the lessons from the migration crisis in Ceuta.
At the end of July, an estimated 80,000 migrants had entered the Spanish exclave from Morocco. According to the government in Madrid, most of the arrivals returned voluntarily to Morocco within a very short time. At least 140 people died trying to reach Ceuta. Aid organizations put the figure significantly higher.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker demanded at the EU summit that there should be more legal options to respond to mass arrivals like those in Ceuta, in particular a right not to have to accept asylum applications under such circumstances.
Greece's government is also pushing to create the legal basis for this option. Greece has suspended the examination of asylum applications twice in the past, most recently in 2025 for three months because of a sharp rise in boat arrivals from Libya to Crete and Gavdos.
The EU migration rules do not actually provide for a full suspension of the right to apply for asylum. The principle of non-refoulement states that a state may not turn back or deport a person to a country where they face persecution, torture or another treatment that violates human rights.

articles.title: France rocked by protests over rising prices as Yellow Vests return
articles.summary: Police clashed with protesters in Paris and other French cities Saturday as thousands demonstrated against rising living costs, stagnant wages and alleged police brutality, revivin...
articles.full_text:
Police clashed with protesters in Paris and other French cities Saturday as thousands demonstrated against rising living costs, stagnant wages and alleged police brutality, reviving the Yellow Vest movement and increasing pressure on President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of the presidential election.
Officers fired tear gas and used water cannons in Paris to disperse groups of demonstrators wearing hoods and face masks who threw fireworks and other objects at police.
Riot police were deployed around Place de la Republique, while authorities closed metro stations and banned some gatherings near government buildings.
Windows at the Paris offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 were broken after protesters threw projectiles at the buildings, according to reports from the scene.
The Interior Ministry said authorities had recorded about 140 protest actions outside the Paris region by shortly after midday, involving more than 32,000 people. Police had detained at least 166 people nationwide.
The demonstrations followed weeks of student-led protests over education funding and police conduct, with labor unions and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement joining calls for higher wages, lower prices and better public services.
The unrest has intensified scrutiny of the government’s response to demonstrations, particularly after several teenagers suffered serious injuries during confrontations with riot police.
In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, masked demonstrators forced their way into the lobby of City Hall after striking the entrance with security barriers.
Some entered the building, and one spray-painted an anarchist symbol on an interior wall before police moved in to disperse them.
Shops and a municipal police station were also damaged. Mayor Benoit Payan described the damage inside City Hall as limited in an interview with French broadcaster BFM TV.
“We’re taking the Bastille,” one demonstrator shouted, invoking the 1789 storming of the Paris fortress that became a defining moment of the French Revolution.
An Agence France-Presse (AFP) photographer also witnessed protesters attacking a police building in Marseille.
“We’re here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality,” said Aude, a masked student who declined to give her surname.
In the western city of Rennes, about 20 people erected a barricade using trash bins and large wooden pallets near a shopping mall.
Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester, said he was angered by what he considered excessive police force against teenagers during recent demonstrations.
“We’ve reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children,” he told AFP.
In central France, about 300 people, including high school students, gathered in Gueret to protest rising prices and stagnant wages.
“At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren’t,” said Franck, a civil servant in his 40s who declined to give his surname.
“We can’t take it anymore, we’re suffocating,” he added.
Authorities also reported violence in Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers, including attempted looting, attacks on police officers, fires involving street furniture and damage to government institutions and media offices.
The demonstrations were organized partly through social media, with supporters seeking to revive the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to planned fuel tax increases and broader concerns about economic inequality.
Named after the high-visibility vests worn by protesters, the movement organized months of demonstrations against Macron’s government, drawing support from workers and rural communities who felt the cost of living was rising faster than their incomes.
Organizers called for renewed protests under the slogan “yellow and youth,” urging teachers, students, workers, pensioners and farmers to participate. More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website established by organizers.
The mobilization coincided with the start of school half-term holidays, as student groups sought to broaden support for protests that began in mid-September. School blockades and demonstrations have focused on education funding and allegations of excessive police force.
The CGT, one of France’s largest labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services.
Authorities imposed restrictions on demonstrations in central Paris, including near the Champs-Elysees, major railway stations and government buildings. Police detained about 60 people in the capital on Saturday morning, according to AFP.
Macron appealed for calm Friday in Brussels, emphasizing that the right to demonstrate did not justify violence or property damage.
“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”
The demonstrations have unfolded amid growing criticism of police tactics during student protests. Thousands of people have been arrested in recent weeks, while hundreds have been injured and some schools have been set on fire during the unrest.
Some of the most serious injuries have involved teenagers struck by police crowd-control weapons. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez suspended the use of a type of stun grenade against young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
The incidents have become a rallying point for protesters who accuse authorities of using disproportionate force to control demonstrations.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday, bringing further international attention to the student movement.
The government faces the challenge of addressing public anger over household costs while preventing further violence. The demonstrations have also become a political issue as France approaches a presidential election campaign in which purchasing power, public services and law enforcement are prominent concerns.
A survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month found that about 45% of French people were concerned about the cost of living and inflation.
Purchasing power has come under pressure, while fuel prices have climbed since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war earlier this year, adding costs for motorists and businesses.
France is also struggling with mounting public debt, which is projected to exceed 120% of gross domestic product next year, roughly double the European Union’s 60% benchmark.
Economists say significantly reducing the debt will require major reforms, potentially including changes to France’s costly pension system. Such proposals have long been politically sensitive, particularly among workers and retirees concerned about their incomes and benefits.
The unrest has given political parties on both the far left and far right an opportunity to position themselves ahead of the presidential race.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and joined a demonstration earlier in the week. Marine Le Pen, whose National Rally party has led opinion polls in the presidential race, has positioned herself in support of the police.
The competing responses reflect the political divisions surrounding the demonstrations, as protesters demand relief from rising prices and improvements to public services while the government faces calls to restore order.

articles.title: US strikes $25M UNICEF deal to avert medicine shortages
articles.summary: The U.S. government has reached an agreement to continue providing some of the world’s poorest countries with free, lifesaving medicines and medical equipment for mothers, infants...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. government has reached an agreement to continue providing some of the world’s poorest countries with free, lifesaving medicines and medical equipment for mothers, infants and young children, following months of uncertainty and supply disruptions.
The U.N. Children’s Fund, or UNICEF, will procure the supplies, a State Department spokesperson told Reuters by email, without disclosing further details. UNICEF said the one-year agreement is worth $25 million.
The funding represents only a fraction of the assistance affected by the Trump administration’s aid cuts and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).
However, the deal should prevent another sudden interruption in supplies that some of the world’s most vulnerable countries depend on as they negotiate new health assistance agreements with Washington.
Nine former U.S. aid officials, nongovernmental organization representatives and government officials told Reuters that an interruption had been a significant concern because the existing contract between the now-defunct USAID and its supplier was due to expire last month.
The agreement covers the procurement and delivery of maternal and child health supplies, as well as some nutrition supplies, to at least 15 countries previously covered by the program, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Mali, UNICEF said.
It follows nearly 18 months of disruption after Washington moved to freeze and then scale back many U.S. aid programs as part of its “America First Global Health Strategy.”
In countries such as Congo, shortages resulting from the disruption have already emerged.
At Nyangezi General Hospital in eastern Congo, health workers said they had run out of lifesaving medications, including oxytocin, used to prevent and treat postpartum hemorrhage, and amoxicillin, an antibiotic used in pediatric care and during childbirth.
“It was a donation we received (previously) from USAID, and at the moment, there is none,” midwife Alice Bulambo told Reuters.
The main government-run warehouse in the area has experienced stockouts for more than a year, said Olivier Kabarati Amani, chief medical officer for the Nyangezi health zone.
As a result, health facilities have been forced to buy medicines at market prices. Over the past six months, “the cost of care has doubled, if not tripled,” Amani said, as the health care system in eastern Congo continues to struggle with Ebola.
The State Department said it “has prioritized ensuring all lifesaving commodities have continued to be made reliably available.”
Maternal and newborn health supplies accounted for less than 1% of the more than $5 billion spent by the USAID Global Health Supply Chain Program between 2016 and 2023, according to the most recently available annual report. The spending was channeled through private contractor Chemonics.
Reuters first reported plans to close the program, which also managed the donation and delivery of supplies to combat malaria and HIV, in April, with aid officials warning that the Sept. 30 shutdown could cause shortages.
The planned closure of the Chemonics supply chain program is part of the broader U.S. global health strategy, which aims to move countries toward self-reliance while scaling back U.S. support and reducing reliance on contractors.
The U.S. has instead signed more than 30 bilateral health aid agreements with recipient countries, including Congo. The agreements require countries to contribute funding and are worth billions of dollars combined.
However, the details of the agreements are still being worked out, and it had been unclear what would fill the gap in the ordering process in the meantime.
Although many countries were already moving toward taking responsibility for their maternal and child health needs, order lead times can reach a year or more, five former USAID officials said.
The Congolese government aims to take over by next year but has struggled with the recent uncertainty, said Polydor Kabila, coordinator of the universal health care program in the president’s office.
Alongside the UNICEF agreement, U.S. authorities have extended the deadline for Chemonics to deliver some key malaria and HIV supplies, the State Department spokesperson told Reuters. The U.S. has also signed an agreement with the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria that allows countries to order new U.S.-funded HIV and malaria supplies through the fund’s ordering platform.
In a statement, UNICEF said it would work with the U.S. to “keep health and nutrition supplies moving so more children receive lifesaving care.” The agency added that no orders had yet been placed but were expected shortly.

articles.title: Egypt's el-Sissi says he will step down in 2030, rules out another term
articles.summary: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi said Saturday that he would leave office when his current term ends in 2030, ruling out any further constitutional amendments to extend his...
articles.full_text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi said Saturday that he would leave office when his current term ends in 2030, ruling out any further constitutional amendments to extend his rule as he also pledged to defend Saudi Arabia’s security and sovereignty if requested.
“The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled,” el-Sissi said during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, according to state-run Al-Ahram newspaper.
“I said that the Egyptian constitution would not be touched,” he added. “This is an entirely settled matter and will not be discussed.”
The 71-year-old president, a former army general who has led Egypt since 2014, is serving a six-year term after winning re-election in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four years to six and allowed Sisi to seek an additional term, enabling him to remain in office until 2030.
The amendments reshaped Egypt’s presidential limits and drew criticism from opponents who warned they would consolidate power in the hands of the president.
El-Sissi came to power in 2013 after the military ousted Mohamed Morsi, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, following mass protests against his rule. El-Sissi subsequently won the presidency in 2014 and has maintained a tight grip on the country’s political system.
His latest remarks appeared aimed at ending speculation about whether he might seek another constitutional change to remain in power beyond his current mandate.
El-Sissi also spoke about the role of the military and the need to prepare a new generation of leaders, linking the armed forces to the protection of Egypt’s constitutional order and state institutions.
He said the constitution defines the military’s responsibility to safeguard democracy, the constitutional framework and the fundamental pillars of the state.
“I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility,” el-Sissi said, referring to efforts to prepare younger generations to take on leadership roles through the Egyptian Military Academy.
The comments did not provide further details about how the transition to new leadership would be managed or what role el-Sissi might play after leaving office.
El-Sissi also declared that Egypt was prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect the kingdom’s security and sovereignty, underscoring Cairo’s stated commitment to the defense of its Gulf partners.
“We will take any measure to protect Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that he would call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorize such action if Riyadh requested it.
“We stand firmly to protect and defend the territories of our brothers in the Gulf,” he added.
El-Sissi did not specify what measures Egypt might take or identify a particular threat that would prompt such a response.

articles.title: India arrests Cockroach movement founder amid election protests
articles.summary: Indian police arrested Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), on Saturday, according to multiple media reports, a day after detaining him ahead of a...
articles.full_text:
Indian police arrested Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), on Saturday, according to multiple media reports, a day after detaining him ahead of a rally in Delhi that drew hundreds of protesters waving national flags and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.
Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and was due to appear before a special executive magistrate on Saturday, broadcasters NDTV and India Today reported.
Delhi police did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.
The CJP, opposition groups and student organizations have staged near-daily protests this month, calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign over a revision of voter lists that they allege favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
More than 130 million voters were deleted from the lists during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favoring any party and said voters who were wrongly removed can re-enroll. The BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was also detained Friday as she tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. She was released Saturday.
"Please, spare the people of India. Impeach Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," Bora told the ANI news agency after her release.
Dipke was detained Friday as he left a house in central Delhi. Police forced him into a police car and drove away after a brief argument.
Dipke had called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders who were detained and sent to jail for five days this week for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
Earlier Friday, police had met with Dipke and warned him against proceeding with the protest.
The Cockroach movement has emerged as a significant source of political pressure on Modi and the BJP during the prime minister's 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by the movement's supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign over exam paper leaks.

articles.title: Pope Leo cleared for discharge 4 days after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, and is expected to deliver his traditional noon blessing Sunday from...
articles.full_text:
Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from the hospital Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, and is expected to deliver his traditional noon blessing Sunday from a window overlooking St. Peter’s Square, the Vatican said.
The 71-year-old pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Tuesday after doctors identified a nodule suspected of being cancerous. The operation confirmed a diagnosis of adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
His personal physician, Luigi Carbone, and surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement released by the Vatican that blood tests, a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning and an assessment of his clinical condition showed he was fit to leave the hospital.
Leo is expected to return to the Vatican in the early afternoon, according to the statement.
The discharge comes earlier than the Vatican’s initial estimate of a weeklong hospital stay and follows several indications that the pope has been recovering well. His audiences had been canceled through Tuesday, but Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the timing of his release would depend on his medical team.
Leo disclosed his condition last Sunday during his traditional appearance before the faithful gathered in St. Peter’s Square, telling them that doctors had found a nodule in his lung that would need to be removed.
Since undergoing surgery, he has continued several official and religious activities from Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, including a telephone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meetings with senior aides and the celebration of Mass in the hospital chapel.
Medical updates from his physician and surgeon have described a positive postoperative recovery, saying Leo has been able to carry out his normal daily activities independently.
The Vatican released the first images of the pope since his surgery Friday, showing him standing at an altar in a hospital chapel wearing green liturgical vestments. Doctors said the latest tests confirmed his continued improvement.
Leo presided over the liturgy himself and distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes attending the service, Bruni said.
During his homily, the pope thanked hospital staff for their daily work caring for sick people and for the attention they had given him during his treatment, Bruni said.
His recovery will be closely watched ahead of a planned trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17. The journey, scheduled to begin about three weeks after his discharge, includes 12 flights and two helicopter trips.
The Vatican has signaled that preparations for the visit are continuing. On Friday, it published the names of journalists accredited to travel aboard the papal plane.
Oncology surgeons say patients can generally be cleared to fly about three weeks after surgery, provided their recovery allows it. Whether Leo will be fit for the demanding trip will depend on his continued progress and his doctors’ assessment.
Medical teams are still awaiting test results that will establish the cancer’s precise molecular and genetic characteristics, determine whether it has spread beyond the removed lung lobe and clarify whether further treatment will be necessary.
